quests.instruction: Choose the best way to approach this.
quests.scene: Your group project is due in two days and one teammate hasn't sent his section. You don't want to start a fight.
options: I've noticed you haven't sent your section yet, and I'm starting to worry that we'll fail because of it.
Since you haven't done your part, I'll do it myself, but you owe me one and I'll mention it to the teacher.
Let's just hope it all comes together in time.
How's your section going? Do you need a hand with anything?
quests.hint: Ask about progress before assuming the worst.
quests.explanation: An open question with an offer of help invites him to share any problem. Accusations, silent takeover, or vague hope avoid a real conversation.
quests.culturalNote: Checking in first is usually seen as fairer than assuming laziness.

quests.scene: In a group meeting, one teammate keeps talking over everyone else and you have an idea you want heard.
options: You keep talking over everyone, and it's making the whole group uncomfortable and unproductive.
It's fine, go with your plan, I'm sure it will turn out well enough for all of us in the end.
I'd like to add an idea before we decide — could I have two minutes?
I've got a better idea, but I'm not sure anyone here is really interested in hearing it at all.
quests.hint: Claim your turn without criticizing anyone.
quests.explanation: Asking for a specific short slot is firm and polite. Criticism, silence, or hinting you're ignored don't get your idea heard.
quests.culturalNote: Requesting a set amount of time is a common way to step into a busy discussion.

quests.instruction: Choose the most effective way to divide the work.
quests.scene: You're leading a three-person team and need to assign research, drafting, and review.
options: I'll assign everything myself, so you can just do what I tell you to do.
Choose whatever you like, we'll figure it out as we go along.
Everyone should do a bit of everything, so it's fair and nobody feels left out.
Let's split it by strengths: Maya takes research, Omar drafts, and I'll do the review. Does that work?
quests.hint: Give a clear plan and invite confirmation.
quests.explanation: Matching tasks to strengths with a check-in is efficient and inclusive. Taking control, leaving it open, or splitting everything equally can waste time.
quests.culturalNote: Leaders often get better buy-in when they propose and ask rather than order.

quests.scene: You got a lower mark than expected on an essay and want to talk to your teacher.
options: Could you help me understand where I lost points on the essay?
I think my grade on the essay is unfair, and I'd like you to look at it again more carefully.
I worked really hard on it, so I don't understand why it wasn't a better grade than this.
Can you just tell me what I need to do to get an A next time?
quests.hint: Ask to understand, not to dispute.
quests.explanation: A learning-focused question invites specific feedback. Challenging the grade or asking for a formula puts the teacher on the defensive.
quests.culturalNote: Teachers usually respond well to questions about how to improve.

quests.scene: Your study group is full, and a classmate asks to join. You'd still like to help her.
options: We're at capacity, but I can share our notes afterward.
Sorry, the group is full, and we work better with fewer people, so please don't take it personally, okay?
Sure, join us, the more the merrier, even if we have to squeeze around the table for the session.
Sorry, the group's already decided.
quests.hint: Say no to the seat but yes to some help.
quests.explanation: A short refusal with a genuine alternative is kind and clear. Over-explaining, saying yes against your limits, or a flat no create discomfort.
quests.culturalNote: Offering another form of help softens a refusal without pretending there's room.

quests.scene: You were ill on Monday and missed an assignment deadline. You're writing to your teacher.
options: I'm sorry the assignment is late, but I've been very busy and I didn't feel very well this week.
The assignment will be late, as I was unwell, so please give me an extension on it, thanks.
I was ill on Monday and missed the deadline. May I submit the assignment tomorrow, with a doctor's note?
Hi, I couldn't finish my assignment on time. Hope that's okay, sorry again for the inconvenience.
quests.hint: State the reason, propose a new date, and offer evidence.
quests.explanation: A clear reason with a specific request and supporting note is easy to approve. Vague, demanding, or casual emails leave the teacher unsure what you need.
quests.culturalNote: Many schools ask for documentation when illness causes a missed deadline.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to raise this.
quests.scene: You spot what looks like an error in your colleague's report before it goes to the client.
options: The totals on page three are wrong, and if the client sees it, the company will look incompetent and careless.
I noticed something odd in your report, but it's probably nothing, so ignore me if it's fine as it is.
Page three's totals look off — can we check them together?
I've already fixed your report, don't worry.
quests.hint: Point to the specific issue and collaborate.
quests.explanation: A short, specific, joint check protects the colleague's dignity and the report. Dramatizing, hedging, or silently fixing all have costs.
quests.culturalNote: Framing an error as something to check together is a common workplace courtesy.

quests.scene: Your manager asks you to take on an extra project, but you're already working at capacity.
options: I'm already overloaded, so I can't take on anything else right now, unfortunately, sorry about that at all.
I can take it on if we move the Friday report. Which one matters more?
Sure, I'll fit it in somehow, even if I have to work late every night this week to do it.
I'd love to, but I have too much on my plate, so maybe you could give it to someone else?
quests.hint: Turn a yes/no into a trade-off.
quests.explanation: Naming the trade-off helps your manager decide priorities. Flat refusal or silent overload doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Asking managers to prioritize is usually welcome.

quests.scene: In a meeting, a colleague proposes an approach you think is weaker than an alternative.
options: That approach won't work, and we've tried it before, so it would be a waste of time and money.
I see the appeal. Could we test both approaches on a small sample before choosing?
Sure, let's go with your approach if everyone else is happy, I don't mind either way at all.
My approach is better, so let's use mine.
quests.hint: Suggest a fair way to compare.
quests.explanation: Proposing a test turns disagreement into evidence. Dismissing, deferring, or insisting keeps the argument personal.
quests.culturalNote: Testing options is a low-conflict way to settle technical disagreements.

quests.scene: A colleague sent your manager an update that presents the dashboard you built as his own work.
options: I did most of that work, and it's not fair that you're taking all the credit for it.
I'll let it go this time, but I hope it won't happen again in future emails.
Thanks for the update. To add context, I built the dashboard, and Priya reviewed it.
Interesting how the dashboard somehow became yours overnight, isn't it?
quests.hint: Correct the record factually, without accusing.
quests.explanation: Adding context in a neutral tone fixes credit without an accusation. Complaints, silent resentment, or sarcasm create conflict.
quests.culturalNote: Factual corrections in shared emails are often better received than accusations.

quests.scene: A new team member usually eats lunch alone. You'd like to include her without making it awkward.
options: We're getting lunch — want to join us?
We usually go to the deli at noon, and you can join if you feel like it or if you happen to be free.
Are you sure you want to eat alone again? It looks a bit lonely to me from where I sit.
Everyone here is quite close, so it might take a while for you to fit in, but it'll happen.
quests.hint: Make it simple and direct.
quests.explanation: A short, warm invitation makes joining easy. Hedged, pitying, or discouraging versions make it harder to say yes.
quests.culturalNote: Direct invitations are more welcoming for newcomers than vague ones.

quests.scene: A teammate's updates arrive late every week and hold up your part.
options: When updates come late, I can't finish my part. Could we agree on a Wednesday cut-off?
You're always late with your updates, and it's holding up the whole team, which isn't fair to us.
Late updates are fine, I'll work around it.
Maybe you should think about how your lateness is affecting everyone else on the team this month.
quests.hint: Describe the effect and propose a fix.
quests.explanation: Linking the delay to your work and proposing a date invites cooperation. Blame or silent acceptance don't change the pattern.
quests.culturalNote: Framing a request around impact is less likely to trigger defensiveness.

quests.scene: During your class presentation, a classmate asks something you can't answer.
options: I haven't studied that part of the topic, so I can't really answer your question at the moment.
Good question — I don't know, but I'll find out and get back to you.
That's outside the scope of this presentation, so I'm not going to cover it today, sorry.
I'm not sure, but I think it might be something like what the textbook says, more or less.
quests.hint: Admit the gap without bluffing.
quests.explanation: Honesty with a follow-up promise builds credibility. Deflecting or guessing weakens it.
quests.culturalNote: Saying 'I don't know, I'll find out' is generally respected in academic and work settings.

quests.scene: During a class talk, your teacher says, 'Can you speak up a little? We can't hear you at the back.'
options: Sorry — is this better?
I'm nervous about speaking, and I find it hard to be louder in front of everyone in the class.
I'll try, but I'm not used to talking in front of a big group of people like this.
I was speaking loud enough, but I'll try to make it a little louder for you.
quests.hint: Respond simply and adjust.
quests.explanation: A short reply plus a quick adjustment keeps the flow. Explaining nerves or arguing draws attention away from the content.
quests.culturalNote: Brief, cooperative responses keep presentations moving.

quests.scene: A classmate asks you to review her essay draft. The introduction is clear, but the third paragraph feels rushed.
options: Your introduction is clear. The third paragraph feels rushed — could you add an example there?
This draft needs a lot of work, and I think you should start again from scratch.
It's good. I don't have anything to add, so I'd just hand it in as it is.
I like it, but there are a few problems that I think other people might notice.
quests.hint: Be specific about what works and what to change.
quests.explanation: Naming a strength and a specific fix is actionable. Vague praise or harsh dismissal doesn't help her improve.
quests.culturalNote: Peer feedback works best when it points to specific lines or sections.

quests.scene: You realize the supplier is delayed and your team may miss Friday's launch. You need to tell your manager.
options: There's a small problem with the supplier, but I'm sure it will resolve by itself before Friday.
The launch is going to fail because the supplier is late, and it's completely out of my control.
I'll handle the supplier, so don't worry.
I'm concerned we'll miss Friday's launch. The supplier's delayed. Here are two options.
quests.hint: Raise the risk early and bring solutions.
quests.explanation: Flagging the issue with options lets your manager act. Minimizing, doom-saying, or hiding the problem removes that chance.
quests.culturalNote: Managers generally prefer early warnings with proposed solutions over late surprises.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to delegate.
quests.scene: You're asking a junior colleague to write the monthly summary for the first time.
options: Do the summary by Thursday, and make sure it's better than last time's version.
Would you like to try the summary? You don't have to, it's fine either way.
I'll do the summary myself, since it's quicker than explaining what I want.
Could you draft the summary? I've attached last month's as a guide, and I'm free to review it Thursday.
quests.hint: Give context, a deadline, and support.
quests.explanation: A clear request with a model and review time sets the junior up to succeed. Commands, vague offers, or doing it yourself don't help them grow.
quests.culturalNote: Good delegation includes a clear task, resources, and a follow-up point.

quests.scene: Your manager finishes explaining a new project and asks, 'Any questions?' You have none right now.
options: No, everything's clear, thanks, I'm sure I'll figure out the rest as I go along on my own.
None right now, but I'll message you if anything comes up.
Actually, I do have a few questions, but I'm not sure they matter much to anyone here.
Not really. I'll ask a colleague if I get stuck during the project, so don't worry.
quests.hint: Say you're fine and leave the door open.
quests.explanation: A short answer with an open door signals confidence and openness. Guessing you'll manage or hinting at hidden questions are less clear.
quests.culturalNote: Managers often value knowing they can be contacted later.

quests.scene: As meeting chair, you're at the time limit with one item left.
options: I'm sorry, we've run over, but this item is really important, so I hope you can all stay a bit longer.
Let's stop here. Nobody has anything useful to add, and it's just wasting everyone's time.
We'll carry on until we've covered everything.
We're at time — let's take the last item offline and send the notes today.
quests.hint: Respect the time and give a next step.
quests.explanation: Closing on time with a plan respects everyone's schedule. Apologizing, criticizing, or overrunning cause frustration.
quests.culturalNote: Ending on time with follow-up is widely seen as good meeting practice.

quests.scene: A colleague makes a mistake in a client meeting and looks embarrassed afterward.
options: That was a pretty big mistake, but I'm sure you'll learn from it, so try not to worry about it too much.
It happens — we'll fix it together.
Don't worry about it. Everybody knows you're new, so nobody will hold it against you at all.
I would have caught that earlier if I had been asked to review your work beforehand.
quests.hint: Reassure briefly and offer to help.
quests.explanation: A short, supportive reply and a shared fix reduce shame. Pointing out the size of the mistake, patronizing, or blaming others don't.
quests.culturalNote: Quick, warm support after a mistake tends to matter more than a long speech.

quests.scene: In a team meeting, a quiet colleague named Sam has relevant experience but hasn't spoken. You'd like to bring him in.
options: Sam, you've worked with this client — what's your take?
Sam, why so quiet? Say something.
Does anyone have any other thoughts? Sam, you can share too, if you like.
Let's hear from Sam, as he's been very quiet, and I'm sure he has something to add.
quests.hint: Invite based on his expertise, not his silence.
quests.explanation: Linking the invitation to his experience makes it a compliment. Pointing out silence or offering weak invitations can embarrass him.
quests.culturalNote: Quiet colleagues often respond well to invitations tied to their expertise.

quests.scene: A friend asks you to sign the attendance sheet for her because she's running late.
options: I would, but I'd get in trouble, and I really can't take a risk like that right now, sorry.
If the teacher finds out, we'll both fail, so please don't ask me to do that again.
I can't sign for you, but I'll share my notes.
Sure, but you owe me a favor, and you have to cover for me next week.
quests.hint: Refuse the rule-breaking and offer a legitimate alternative.
quests.explanation: A short refusal with a real alternative stays honest and friendly. Excuses based on risk or trading favors keep the request alive.
quests.culturalNote: Signing for someone else is usually considered a serious breach in schools.

quests.scene: Your study partner keeps cancelling at the last minute. You'd like a clear answer.
options: You keep cancelling, so I don't think you really want to study with me.
It's fine, cancel whenever you want, I'll just study by myself as usual.
I've set aside Thursday for us. Should I plan on it, or should I study on my own?
I'm starting to think this isn't working, so maybe we shouldn't study together any more.
quests.hint: Ask for a clear commitment without blaming.
quests.explanation: Naming the time and giving her a clear choice invites honesty. Accusations or silent acceptance keep the pattern going.
quests.culturalNote: A specific plan makes it easier for people to say 'yes' or 'not this time'.

quests.scene: Your teacher hands back an exam with a harsh comment about your writing.
options: I don't agree with the comments, and I think the marking wasn't very fair at all.
Thank you for the comments. Could I come to office hours to work on the areas you mentioned?
I studied hard, so I'm really upset that the comments were so negative about my work.
Okay. I'll try to do better next time, even though I did my best already.
quests.hint: Turn criticism into a plan.
quests.explanation: Thanking her and asking for help shows you can use feedback. Arguing, venting, or minimal acceptance don't lead to improvement.
quests.culturalNote: Office hours are widely available for exactly this kind of follow-up.

quests.scene: A teammate has been working late every night and seems close to burnout.
options: You look exhausted. Maybe you should think about taking some time off from work.
You've been buried lately — how are you holding up? Can I take something off your plate?
We're all busy, so you'll just have to push through the busy period like the rest of us.
If you need anything, just let me know, whenever, no pressure at all, okay?
quests.hint: Notice, ask, and offer something specific.
quests.explanation: Checking in and offering concrete help shows care. Comments on appearance, dismissal, or vague offers don't help.
quests.culturalNote: Specific offers are more likely to be accepted than open-ended ones.

quests.scene: Working remotely, you're sending your manager a weekly status update.
options: Working on it. Should be fine, more soon.
I've done a lot this week, but there's still plenty to do, so it's hard to say when it will be finished.
Things are progressing well, although I'm waiting on a few other things to get done first.
Update: the draft is done, testing is in progress, and I need Maria's data by Thursday to finish.
quests.hint: Give status, next step, and what you need.
quests.explanation: A clear status with a dependency and a date lets the manager help. Vague updates leave gaps.
quests.culturalNote: Remote teams rely on clear written updates.

quests.scene: You learn indirectly that a launch date changed, and your team wasn't told.
options: Why wasn't I told about the launch date, and who decided to leave me out of it?
I guess I'm not important enough to be told when decisions are made around here.
I heard the launch date changed. I'd like to be included in those decisions, as it affects my team.
It's fine, I'll adapt to whatever date you choose, I always do.
quests.hint: State the impact and ask for inclusion.
quests.explanation: Naming the effect on your team and asking to be included is assertive but calm. Accusations or resignation don't change the process.
quests.culturalNote: Asking for inclusion in decisions is easier when tied to the team's needs.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to handle this.
quests.scene: You're presenting your team's results and one member contributed very little.
options: I'll present the results and acknowledge everyone's contributions, and afterwards we'll agree how we split tasks next time.
I'll present, and I'll mention that some people didn't do their fair share of the work.
I'll present quietly and put everyone's names on the slides, no matter what they did.
Since I'm doing the presenting, I should get most of the credit for the work.
quests.hint: Handle credit fairly and address the problem privately.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging everyone publicly and dealing with workload later avoids humiliation and resentment. Public blame or hoarding credit both harm the team.
quests.culturalNote: Public praise with private feedback is a widely recommended approach.

quests.scene: Your manager announces a change you're not sure about.
options: I don't think this change is a good idea, and I doubt it will work in practice at all.
It seems like a decent idea, but I would like to see more details on paper first.
We tried something like this before, and it didn't work, so I'm not optimistic.
What problem is this change meant to solve, and how will we measure whether it works?
quests.hint: Ask questions that clarify purpose and success.
quests.explanation: Purpose and measurement questions show engagement without opposing. Criticism or vague hesitation don't move the conversation.
quests.culturalNote: Constructive questions are a common way to voice concerns.

quests.scene: You're moving to another team and want to leave your current one well prepared.
options: I've left my files in the shared folder, so you can find whatever you need in there.
I've written up handover notes and I'm available for questions until the end of next week.
I'm sure you'll manage without me. The team is strong, and I've already told them everything.
I'd rather not be contacted after I leave, so please read the notes before asking me anything.
quests.hint: Prepare the team and stay reachable for a set time.
quests.explanation: Notes plus availability for a defined period support the team without an open-ended burden. Leaving files, assuming, or refusing contact create problems.
quests.culturalNote: Handover practices vary, but time-limited availability is common.
